opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those terms that's gotten stretched in a lot of directions, and I try to be fairly liberal about it while still keeping it from meaning nothing. The way I usually put it is that a world model is some representation inside a system that encodes the state of the world, or some piece of the world, and that can be used to predict how that state changes, either over time or in response to actions. If you have that, I'm pretty happy to call it a world model, even if it's partial, approximate, or only covers a narrow domain.

What I'm not willing to do is make it all-or-nothing. A lot of the debate, especially around language models, gets framed as "do LMs have a world model or not?" I don't think that's a useful question. Any reasonable system has world models of some things and not others, at some levels of fidelity and not others. A model might track which entities exist in a story, what properties they have, and how those change as you describe events, and you can find that in the representations and even intervene on it. That's a world model of that little discourse situation. It might be terrible at intuitive physics or long-horizon planning. Both can be true.

So the boundaries I care about are about what the representation supports. Is it just correlational, or can you read out something like a state? Does it update coherently as new information comes in? Can you intervene on it and get the downstream behavior you'd predict? Those causal and interventional criteria are, for me, what separate a world model from a bag of surface statistics that happen to give the right answer on a benchmark.

The other thing I'd add is that "world" can be a bit misleading. Often what we really mean is a model of a situation, the state of a conversation, the beliefs and goals of the people in it, the objects being discussed. Some of the most interesting questions for language are about those more local, communicative world models, not a full simulation of physical reality.

r001.rationale: The response says a world model may cover only “a narrow domain” or “some piece of the world,” and gives a small discourse situation as an example.

r002.rationale: The response describes criteria it uses to distinguish a world model from surface statistics, but does not express uncertainty about where that boundary lies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I try to be pretty deflationary about it. There's a version of the term "world model" that's become almost a slogan, where it's supposed to mean something like a complete, faithful, interpretable simulation of the environment sitting inside the network, and I think if that's the bar, then basically nothing has a world model, including people. What I actually care about is a more operational notion. If a system has internal state that tracks some latent variable in the environment that isn't directly given in its inputs, and that state is actually used downstream to make predictions or decisions, and crucially, if I intervene on that state the behavior changes in the way you'd expect, then I'm comfortable saying it's modeling that aspect of the world.

So the boundary for me is really about causal role rather than representational richness. The toy example people in my group have looked at is something like a model trained on transcripts of a board game, where you can show there's a linear encoding of the board state and that editing that encoding changes the model's moves. That's a world model of the board, in a very narrow sense. It says nothing about whether the same system has a model of anything else. And I think that's the right way to talk about it: not "does GPT-whatever have a world model, yes or no," but "which variables does it track, how reliably, and under what distribution of inputs."

Where I get more cautious is in two places. One is when the representation is there but it's not actually doing anything, so you can decode it with a probe but the model's behavior doesn't depend on it. I don't want to call that a world model, that's just a correlate. The other is the question of generality. A lot of these models have what you might call local world models that work beautifully inside the training distribution and then fall apart the moment you change the rules slightly, and the interesting scientific question is whether that fragility is a fundamental property or just a reflection of how we're training them right now.

So I'd rather keep the term and make it precise and graded than throw it out or reserve it for some idealized object we've never built.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a system can model a specific aspect of the world, giving a board state as a narrow example, and says this does not imply it models anything else.

r002.rationale: The candidate offers a criterion based on causal role and notes limits of local models, but does not express uncertainty about where to draw the boundary between a model and a collection of heuristics.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d use the term fairly broadly, but then try to be precise about what particular claim we’re making. A world model doesn’t have to be a complete simulator of everything. It might be a model of a very small part of the world: where an object is, what somebody knows, or what will happen if you take a particular action.

The distinction I care about is between a system that can reproduce patterns in observations and a system that represents something about the process that generated those observations. Those aren’t mutually exclusive—a prediction objective might give you exactly that kind of representation. But being good at prediction doesn’t, by itself, tell us what representation you’ve learned.

So I’d want to ask: can you use this model when the circumstances change? Can you reason about something you haven’t directly observed? If you intervene, does it predict the consequences correctly? Those are ways of making the claim more concrete.

And I don’t think there has to be a sharp boundary. A system might have a useful model of some aspects of the world and a very shallow understanding of others. Saying which aspects, and what evidence we have, seems more informative than deciding whether the whole system gets the label.

r001.rationale: It says a world model can cover “a very small part of the world,” with examples such as an object’s location or what someone knows.

r002.rationale: It says there need not be a sharp boundary and describes systems as having useful models of some aspects but shallow understanding of others, expressing uncertainty about where modelhood ends.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to use the term fairly broadly. A world model is some internal representation that lets you predict things about the environment, especially things that you haven’t directly observed. If I take an action, what’s going to happen? If I learn something about one part of a situation, what does that tell me about another part?

I don’t think that representation has to look like a little simulator, with explicit objects and physical laws. It could be distributed across the activations of a neural network. But I do want the term to carry some predictive content. Being able to decode a fact from a representation is weaker evidence than showing that the system can use that representation to make a new prediction, or reason about what would happen if something changed.

So the interesting question for me is less whether a system has a world model, as a binary property, and more: what aspects of the world does it model, under what circumstances can it use that model, and where does it break down?

r001.rationale: The response discusses which aspects of the world a system models, but does not clearly state that a world model can be limited to a specific, narrow domain.

r002.rationale: The response questions treating world models as a binary property, but does not express uncertainty about the boundary between a model and a collection of heuristics.
